pr_body:
This PR removes `LogicalTypeId::JSON`, and moves the logical type to the JSON extension, just like other custom types like `INET`. This requires a bump in the storage version, as `LogicalTypeId::JSON` is in our storage version test.

This also means that for some data formats we will now return `LogicalTypeId::VARCHAR` instead, but casting to `JSON` is free, and possible only if the JSON extension is installed.

Besides that, this PR also implements `read_json_objects` and `read_ndjson_objects`. These were implemented using a macro for the CSV reader before, but are now implemented and are much faster. The `read_ndjson_objects` function now reads newline-delimited JSON data, and is able to do so in parallel. The `read_json_objects` function can read any type of JSON data, even non-newline-delimited, but does so single-threadedly. We should be able to detect whether the JSON is newline-delimited or not automatically, but I will do that in a future PR.

I've generated the `lineitem` table at SF1 as a newline-delimited JSON file, which is around 2GB. I ran this query:
```sql
create temporary table test as select * from read_ndjson_objects('lineitem.json');
```

Here are the timings:

| Implementation | Timing [s] |
| :- | :- |
| Old | 3.795 |
| `read_json_objects` (new) | 4.371 |
| `read_ndjson_objects` (new) | **0.730** |

I'm happy to receive any feedback on this. This was my first `TableFunction` implementation, so I am sure there are some things that I missed.

@wonb168 This PR implements `read_json_objects`, which we already had before but was implemented as a macro that used the CSV reader.

These improvements speed up the ingestion of JSON and should prepare us for a future PR where we automatically detect the JSON schema and convert it to tabular data. Until then, we don't have this, and you can use `json_transform` to supply the schema yourself.

I've just encountered a problem while trying to fix #5798 in this PR. I'm parsing using the `YYJSON_READ_INSITU` flag to reduce memory allocations (allocations were slowing down reads by A LOT), but I cannot properly restore the input string as I thought I could. I am currently looking for other options to reduce allocations. Just documenting this here, this needs to be fixed before this PR is ready.

Had to remove the `YYJSON_READ_INSITU` flag sadly, although the performance diff is not a big deal. Following the discussion at [ibireme/yyjson#100](https://github.com/ibireme/yyjson/issues/100) I did a big refactor to the JSON extension, and we now use a custom allocator everywhere.

The benchmark I used earlier is now actually < 1s on my laptop! Big thanks to the author of yyjson.
The allocation improvements seem to bring a 20-30% performance benefit to other functions such as `json_extract` as well.

Thanks for the feedback! I think I've implemented all of it. I was able to reproduce the 32-bit issue in a Docker container, and I've managed to fix it there, so I hope CI is happy now too. Fingers crossed 🤞
I've also fixed #5960 in this PR

issue_context.title: json_contains only checks value from second parameter
issue_context.body:
### What happens?

My second argument to json_contains has the same value as the first parameter, but a different key. I would expect this to return false, since the entire json in the second parameter is not present in the first.

### To Reproduce

```sql
select json_contains(json('{"key":"value"}'),json('{"blah":"value"}')) as my_json_contains;
```
| my_json_contains |
|------------------|
| true             |

Windows

0.6.1 and 0.6.2-dev1283

I copied this from the CSV reader. Do we need to open the file to get the file size? I didn't see any other way.

The parquet reader opens only the first file and then estimates the total number of row groups for all files by multiplying the number of row groups in the first file by the number of files. Would this be OK here? This would be slightly problematic if we read a small file (which would be read using 1 thread) first and then a large file (which would require all threads), as we would underestimate the thread count by a lot.
That is true - perhaps it is indeed better to always launch `n` tasks as it is unlikely to hurt much.
